title: The rich Stoic
hook: critics then and now point out that Seneca preached simplicity while very wealthy (On the Happy Life 17)

segments.voice: Yesterday: ratio, Seneca's last surviving letter. Your line was reason's good. Which choice did reason make? Day four hundred ninety-one.

For about sixty days, a man has been telling us that bread and water are enough, that the parade of silver is only a show, that gold ceilings hide a dusty soul. Here's what he owned. Country estates. Gardens near Rome. Loans across the empire, his critics said. One accuser, as Tacitus reports, put his gains in the hundreds of millions of sesterces, a sum hard to translate into anything we'd recognize. Five days ago we promised to look at this honestly. Seneca, to his credit, looks at it too. Today: the rich Stoic.
screen: `BREAD AND WATER ARE ENOUGH, HE SAID.` → `ESTATES, GARDENS, LOANS.` → `HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF SESTERCES.`

segments.voice: First, the critics, then. Tacitus reports that a senator named Suillius attacked Seneca in public: how, he asked, had this philosopher gathered three hundred million sesterces in four years of royal friendship? Through lending, Suillius said, that drained Italy and the provinces. A much later historian, Cassius Dio, even blames Seneca's loans in Britain for stirring up a revolt there. Historians argue over how far to trust either accuser. Suillius was settling scores, and Dio is often hostile. Second, Seneca's own book. In On the Happy Life he puts the charge in his critics' mouths himself: why do you talk one way and live another? You praise poverty and keep estates. You praise simplicity and serve fine wine. He doesn't skip the question. Third, his answer. A wise person, he argues, isn't forbidden wealth; the wealth simply mustn't own the person. Riches should sit in the house, not in the heart. If they vanished, the wise person would lose things, not themselves. Fourth, minding the gap. Is that a fair answer or a convenient one? Readers have argued about it ever since, and this path won't settle it. What's useful is the shape of the problem. Anyone who names a value can be asked Seneca's question. He at least wrote the accusation down in his own book, where every reader could see it.
screen: `SUILLIUS: 300 MILLION IN FOUR YEARS.` · `SENECA WRITES THE CHARGE HIMSELF.` · `IN THE HOUSE, NOT IN THE HEART.` · `THE QUESTION ANYONE CAN BE ASKED.` · then, large: `MIND THE GAP.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you say you value. Patience, honesty, family first, simple living. Now look, gently, at last week. Where did your life match it? Where didn't it? Don't build a case against yourself, and don't build a defense. Just see the gap the way you'd see the distance between two stepping stones. Then ask one question: what's one step that would close it by a few inches? The bell holds the time.
Divitiae. Latin for riches, which Seneca says the wise may hold, as long as the riches don't hold them. Today's word.
Your line: mind the gap. Take the few-inch step you named today. And when you notice someone else's gap, remember Seneca wrote his own down. Day four hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Some readers of Seneca wrestle openly with his wealth, using the tension to examine the gaps between their own stated values and their daily lives.

fork.setup: you're Seneca, and critics say you praise poverty while living in luxury. what do you write?
options: state the charge plainly and argue riches belong in the house, not the heart.
fork.reveal: he puts the accusation in his own book and answers it, an answer readers still argue over.

original.note: Latin, 'riches': which Seneca says the wise may hold, as long as the riches don't hold them.

trapdoor: what you thought: Seneca was a hypocrite, end of story.
what it means: he was very rich, faced the charge in his own book, and argued wealth may be held without being served.
what a scholar hears: the Stoics classed wealth as a 'preferred indifferent', neither good nor bad in itself, which is the theory behind Seneca's defense.

notes: Tacitus, Annals 13.42: Suillius' charge of 300 million sesterces in four years of imperial friendship, through usury in Italy and the provinces. Confirm the figure and wording.
Cassius Dio 62.2: Seneca's recalled loans in Britain named among causes of Boudica's revolt. Confirm.
On the Happy Life 17 (the critics' charge, including estates and wine) and 21–26 (wealth in the house, not the heart; riches serve the wise, rule the fool). Confirm.
Hook's 'gardens famous across Rome' (horti Senecae, Juvenal 10.16) and 'hundreds of millions': confirm or soften.
'Preferred indifferent' (proēgmenon) is standard Stoic theory; confirm trapdoor.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the 300-million figure is now credited to the accuser Suillius via Tacitus, not to 'a historian'; cut 'among the richest people alive' (hook, screen, word) and 'two thousand years'; fixed the garbled 'it simply mustn't own them'; the close no longer tells the listener they have a gap.
